response.title: Reading a Stream Together
response.passage:
When students at Brookfield High began checking a stream near their town, they hoped to give the community useful information, not to prove that the water was either clean or dirty. Four students cooperated with a park worker and two nearby residents. They agreed to visit the same three points on two different days and to record what they saw before discussing what it might mean.

On their first visit, the students arrived the morning after heavy rain. Near the bridge, a fallen leaf traveled quickly past a stone at the water’s edge. The park worker explained that rain upstream can change the flow even when the sky above the stream is clear. The students also observed the water’s color, but their teacher reminded them that clear water alone could not show whether it was safe. They collected samples and wrote down the time and location for each one.

The group used the same thermometer at every point. At the first stop, however, one student left it in direct sunlight while writing notes. Its reading was higher than the next two readings. Rather than choosing the result they liked best, the students moved the thermometer into the shade and measured again. The new reading matched the other two. Their teacher said that a reliable record depended on careful, repeated measurements, not on a single number.

A week later, after several dry days, the team returned. The water’s surface looked almost still, but a leaf placed beside the same stone moved steadily downstream. The current was slower than it had been after the rain, yet it had not stopped. This time, the students took longer to finish because they checked each other’s notes and compared the same locations. In their report, they described the two visits separately and explained that the different weather might have affected what they observed. They did not claim that the stream had become safer or more polluted. Instead, they recommended more visits before drawing a firm conclusion. The park worker added that the students’ careful record would help decide where to focus future checks.

items.answer: The students combined careful teamwork with caution about what two visits could show.
distractors: The students tried to prove that the stream was unsafe after the rain.
The students let the park worker make every measurement and write the report.
The students compared their results mainly to decide which class had the best team.
items.question: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

items.answer: The first reading was higher, so they repeated it in the shade and checked it against the others.
distractors: The first reading was lower, so they accepted it without taking more measurements.
The thermometer gave the same reading at every point, so they stopped using it.
The students changed thermometers because the park worker said theirs could not be trusted.
items.question: Why did the students measure the temperature again at their first stop?

items.answer: The rain may have contributed to the faster flow on the first visit.
distractors: The dry weather made the stream stop flowing before the second visit.
The clear appearance of the water proved that rain had made it safer.
The students’ notes show that the current was faster during the dry week.
items.question: What can readers infer by combining the weather details with the students’ observations of the leaves?

items.answer: The moving leaf showed that water was still flowing downstream.
distractors: The nearly still surface showed that the water had stopped moving completely.
The leaf’s movement showed that the stream was flowing faster than after the rain.
The leaf stayed beside the stone, showing that the students had chosen a point without moving water.
items.question: During the second visit, what showed that the current had not stopped?
